answer.text: Options with longest time to expiry

explanation.text: The Logic: Gamma measures how rapidly an option's delta changes as the underlying moves. For at-the-money options, delta is around 0.5 and is most sensitive to underlying price moves, so gamma peaks at the money. For deep in-the-money options, delta is close to 1 and barely moves, so gamma is low; for deep out-of-the-money options, delta is close to 0 and again barely moves, so gamma is also low. Time to expiry has the opposite effect — for ATM options, gamma actually rises sharply as expiry approaches, so longest-expiry options do not have the highest gamma. The Trap: "Longest time to expiry" is the most tempting wrong answer because investors associate long-dated options with the highest values of most Greeks (like vega and theta) — but gamma behaves the opposite way for ATM options. Note: A direct statement that gamma is highest for ATM options, with the comparison to deep ITM, deep OTM and longest-expiry options, is not present on the NISM Series I Currency Derivatives workbook pages checked (which define gamma with a single ATM put example); the framing above reflects the standard Black-Scholes options-Greeks behaviour rather than a workbook citation.
